about: Dorestad (Dorestat, now Wijk bij Duurstede), the player's home port, 793 to 863 and what is left of it to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/dorestad.md and the spine (Design/content/spine.json). A draft in the game's own file, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified.

ports.summary: Dorestad is the Frankish king's toll port and mint in the north: three kilometres of timber houses and earth dams along the west bank of the Crooked Rhine, just below the fork where the Lek leaves it, with no wall round any of it. Frisian shippers bring Rhine wine, Mayen quernstones, Badorf pots and glass down the river and carry cloth, combs, salt and fish back up, and the king's men take a tenth of every sale. It is your home: the count holds your debt here, the widow on the dam holds your goods, and everybody on the bank knows whose boat yours is.
ports.seasons: No fair has a day here: ships lie between the dams and wait for a cargo, a wind or company. The winter and spring floods drown the low ground and in a hard winter the river carries ice; in high summer half the comb of dams stands dry and the big ships lie off the heads on the sand. The new wine comes down after the vintage, about Martinmas, and the reckoning with the count is at Michaelmas.

history.text: In these years Pippin the mayor beat Radbod, king of the Frisians, at the fort of Dorestad, and the Franks kept the fork of the river. (The year is not exact.)
history.source: Fredegar's continuator, by L. van der Tuuk, http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html (the year (?))

history.text: This year Winfrid, who was afterwards called Boniface, crossed from London to Dorestad with a fair wind and found Radbod at war with the Franks.
history.source: Willibald, Life of Boniface c. 4, by Design/content/ships.md

history.text: On the eighth of June King Charles gave to Saint Martin's of Utrecht the church called Upkirika above Dorestad, with a hundred perches of land, the bank due on the Lek, and the island eastward between Rhine and Lek.
history.source: Oorkondenboek Sticht Utrecht I no. 48, by http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html

history.text: This year the king freed an abbey's ships of the toll at Dorestad, as at Quentovic, Rouen, Amiens and Maastricht.
history.source: Charter for Saint-Germain-des-Pres, 779, by http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html and story/unlocks_793.json

history.text: About this year Alcuin sent a letter in verse down the Rhine: at Utrecht honey, porridge and butter, since Frisia pours neither oil nor wine; then hoist sail and flee Dorestad, for Hrotberct the black, the greedy merchant, will give no lodging.
history.source: Alcuin, carmen 4, MGH Poetae I 220-223 (our rendering): https://sourcebook.stanford.edu/text/alcuin_song_4_go_quickly/

history.text: This year there was great hunger in Francia. At Dorestad the mint still struck the light penny with CARO/LVS on one face and DOR/STAT with an axe on the other.
This year the king's new heavy penny with his monogram was ordered taken in every place, and the old light pennies had to be brought to the mint.

On the eighteenth of March the emperor Louis confirmed to Saint Martin's its tenth of the king's income and its banks in Dorestad: its men there owed no bank due and no 'giscot', no one might lodge in their houses, and no one might seize their goods at death.
history.source: Oorkondenboek Sticht Utrecht I no. 56, by http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html and H6.html

history.text: This year Martinmas was the last day on which the old pennies could be paid.
This year Harald the Dane, baptised at Mainz, went home down the Rhine by Dorestad with the monk Ansgar, in a ship with two cabins that the bishop of Cologne had lent them.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 7, tr. C. H. Robinson 1921

history.text: This year the emperor's own merchants, free of toll everywhere else, were told they still owed the tenth at Quentovic, at Dorestad and at the passes.
This year the Danes came by Utrecht to Dorestad and plundered it. They killed some, carried others off captive, and burned a part.
This year the heathen men came to Dorestad again and wasted it.
This year they came a third time. Antwerp and Witla at the mouth of the Maas were burned.
This year, after they had taken Walcheren on the seventeenth of June, the Danes came to Dorestad and took tribute. The emperor hurried to Nijmegen, blamed disobedience and ordered a fleet.
About this year Dorestad was burned with two other villages while the emperor Lothar looked on from Nijmegen, and the Danes held Dorestad and the Betuwe.
history.source: Annales Xantenses 846; Annales Fuldenses; Annales Bertiniani 847: http://www.gjallar.nl/bronnen_AX.html

history.text: This year Rorik the Dane came by the mouths of the Rhine with a fleet, and Lothar, who could not drive him out, granted him Dorestad and other counties, on terms: to pay in the king's dues and keep the pirates off.

About this year Catla of Birka came to Dorestad with the silver of her dead mother Frideburg and gave it to the poor and the holy places. In the same years Swedes said the way to Dorestad was beset by pirates.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20 and c. 27, tr. C. H. Robinson 1921 (the year (?))

history.text: This year Rorik sailed to the Eider with his fleet, and while he was gone other Danes stormed Dorestad.

This year, in January, in a winter of floods, the Danes came up the Rhine to Dorestad. Frisian merchants who had fled to a large estate were killed there. The Danes left on Rorik's advice and went on up the river.
This year the people the annals call Cokingi drove Rorik out of Frisia.
This year Rorik swore faith to King Louis. He is not heard of again.
About this year the harbour was given up: the river had left the dams, and flood clay lay over the old plots.
history.source: http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/H2.html and H8.html (Van Es and Verwers)

history.text: On Saint John's day King Zwentibold gave Saint Martin's men at Deventer and Tiel the freedom they had had 'in Dorestadio'.
On the first of April King Otto named it in a charter: 'the estate once called Dorsteti, but now Wik'.
In these years the church and estate of Wijk passed from Adela of Hamaland to Archbishop Heribert of Cologne and his abbey of Deutz.
This year King Henry confirmed to the bishop of Utrecht the banks of Dorestad, nearly two hundred years after the last ship lay at them.

eras.text: The hungry year. Bread is dear, the poor crowd the church door, and grain is the cargo everyone asks for. The mint still strikes the light penny; from midsummer 794 only the heavy one passes, the king's price for grain is cried on the dams, and the count's steward checks every measure against the new one. English ports are shut to Frankish ships and finished quernstones pile up unsold.

The king's port at its work. The quarrel with the English ends in 796 and the stones move again. The count is away with the host most summers; in 797 boats and men are pressed to haul the king's ships into Saxony, and in 810 every boat is called out against Godfred's two hundred sails. Dirhams begin to turn up in the purses of men from the north.

The good years, as rich as the place will ever be. Great storehouses stand on the newest ground of the dams, which are built further out every few years after the river. The penny shows a ship with the town's name (812 to 818). In 826 a baptised Danish king goes by with a monk called Ansgar. The children of the people you knew hold the dam heads.

The raid years. A fleet comes up from Utrecht in 834, in 835 and in 836; in 837 it takes tribute; about 847 the place burns in sight of the emperor at Nijmegen. Between raids loot is sold cheap and houses are mended. People put their silver in the ground and go armed to the boats. From Pentecost to Lammas nobody sleeps well.

Rorik's town. A Dane holds Dorestad for the king and his man takes the tenth on the dam; the fleets pass by while he is at home. The churches are full again and the poor are many: Catla of Birka brings her mother's silver for them. The pennies are poor ones in Lothar's name. The river is leaving: the heads stand in mud. In 857 other Danes storm the town; in January 863 the last sack comes with the flood.

The leaving. The houses that are left sell their timber. The merchants go to Tiel, Deventer and Utrecht and take the name of Dorestad's freedom with them. Rorik is driven out in 867, comes back, and is last heard of in 873. A few boats still lie where the dams reach water.
Clay over the plots. The harbour is given up. Cattle graze the dams; posts stand out of the grass in rows. Men of Tiel and Deventer say 'as we had it at Dorestad' when they argue a toll.
Wik: a village with a church and a lord's estate on the bank of a small river. From 1016 it is the abbey of Deutz's. Children find green pennies with a ship on them after the plough.

sites.name: The dam heads
sites.see: A comb of earth-and-wattle dams runs out from the bank road into the brown river, each as wide as a cart is long, storehouses with reed roofs standing on them and black ditches between. Your boat lies between two dams with the small craft; the big ships lie at the heads or on the sand beyond. Tow-ropes creak, porters shout in Frisian, and it smells of wet oak, tar and river mud.
sites.source: Hoogstraat excavation 1967-77: dams 6 to 7 m wide and up to 200 m long, ditches 4 m, boats of 2 to 3 m beam between (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md; Van Es and Verwers)

sites.name: The king's toll post
sites.see: Where the bank road meets the first dam a post with the king's mark stands by an open shed. A man with a tally stick sits on an upturned cask, a clerk with a wax tablet beside him, two spearmen leaning in the shade. Behind them carts wait and a line of skippers stands with their hands in their belts.
sites.source: The tenth (decima) and the bank due (ripaticum): charters of 777 and 815, the precept of 828. Where the toll was taken is not known: this place for it is ours (?)

sites.name: The selling on the dams
sites.see: There is no market place: goods are sold off the decks and at the storehouse doors, all down the dams. Wine casks from up the river stand in rows, grey lava querns lie stacked like loaves, bolts of cloth hang over a rail, and a woman sells eels from a wicker car in the ditch. Scales swing, men spit on their palms and strike hands.
sites.source: Trade on dams and ships, no market square: http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/H6.html; wicker fish cars: H11.html; the goods: dossier 4

sites.name: Thiadburg's storehouse
sites.see: A long storehouse of split oak on the newest ground of a dam, its door facing the water, a ring of keys hanging at the belt of the woman who stands in it. Inside, in the half dark, casks, bales under hides and a row of sealed sacks with tally sticks tied to their necks. A cat sleeps on the wool.
sites.source: Large warehouses on the newest ground of the dams, c. 750-830 (Van Es and Verwers; H8.html). The widow is the spine's (cast.thiadburg)

sites.name: Thiadbod's dam head
sites.see: The best berth on the river: the longest dam, new posts, a plank way wide enough for two men with a cask between them. A broad sea-going ship lies at its head with her sail furled in a red cover, and men who are paid by the year sit on the wine waiting to be told to move it.
sites.source: Paired dams on plots 18 m wide, lengthened as the river moved (Van Es and Verwers). The rival is the spine's (cast.thiadbod)

sites.name: The king's mint
sites.see: A low house with a guarded door near the old fort, smoke coming from under the eaves. Inside a man in a leather apron sets a silver blank between two iron dies on a stump and strikes once; a boy sweeps the floor into a pan because the dust is silver. On the bench: scales, a touchstone, a heap of other kings' coins waiting for the fire.
sites.source: With Melle the busiest mint of the kingdom in the later 8th century; foreign coin had to be reminted (http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/B5.html). Its place is not known: 'the upper town' is the game's (?)

sites.name: Saint Martin's, the upper church
sites.see: A timber church with a shingle roof on the higher ground by the fork, inside the grey stump of the Romans' fort where the Lek leaves the Rhine. The poor sit along its south wall out of the wind. From the door you see both rivers and every sail on them; inside it is dark, and smells of wax, wet wool and the one lamp.
sites.source: The Upkirika, 'above Dorestad', given to Utrecht in 777 (OSU 48): the one church named here. It and the fort were later lost to the river. That it was of timber is ours (?)

sites.name: The lord's hall at De Geer
sites.see: Five hundred paces north-west of the houses, a long ditched enclosure and in it a hall with a bowed roof, horses tied outside, shields along the wall. By the door hang bundles of notched sticks, one for every debt in the district. Dogs lie in the sun; a thin grey man counts something aloud in dozens.
sites.source: De Geer: an enclosure 85 by 380 m with a hall 10 by 22 m, a lord's seat from the early 8th to the mid 9th century (H5.html). The count is the game's: the attested officers are the king's procurators

sites.name: The breaking beach
sites.see: Below the last dam the bank is bare sand, littered with rust-red ship nails. An old clinker hull lies on her side with half her planks off, and beside her a new keel on blocks, pale as bread. Adzes knock, a pitch pot smokes, and wool for caulking dries on a rack.
sites.source: Ship nails and a dismantled clinker hull on the beach at the dam heads; the keel-ship fragment with wool caulking, after c. 739 (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md; Design/content/ships.md)

sites.name: The row behind the bank road
sites.see: Narrow houses stand gable to the road, each with its work at the door: a man sawing antler into comb teeth, a woman at an upright loom with clay weights swinging, a boy drilling amber, a quern cutter grey to the elbows dressing a black stone from Mayen. Between the houses are wells lined with old wine casks.
sites.source: Houses 5 to 6 by 12 to 16 m; workshops for combs, amber, querns, iron, cloth (2,889 loomweights), glass beads; some 650 wells lined with Rhenish casks (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md; H9.html)

sites.name: Aldswith's house
sites.see: A house on the bank road with its door open and a bush of green leaves tied over it. Inside one long room, a hearth in the middle of the floor with the smoke going out through the roof, benches along both walls, a gaming board cut into the table. Shipmen of four tongues drink ale out of Badorf pots and a dog cracks a bone under the bench.
sites.source: A lodging (hospitium) at Dorestad: Rimbert c. 20. Gaming pieces, a swan-bone flute, amber lyre bridges and dog-gnawed kitchen bones from the digs (H9.html). The green bush as an ale-sign is later custom (?)

sites.name: The graves at De Heul
sites.see: Fenced plots of low mounds lying east and west under old alders, and among them a small timber building with three coffins of white stone beside it. Near the gate is the only stone well in Dorestad, built of the Romans' grey tuff. It is quiet; rooks, wind in the alders, and somebody's mother sweeping leaves off a grave.
sites.source: De Heul, late 7th to early 9th century: fenced plots, a building 14 by 8 m with three limestone sarcophagi, the one stone well, of Roman tuff (H10.html)

people.name: Ravn
people.trait: Dry and watchful; keeps his word and his own counsel; pious to the old gods without talking of them; sets riddles instead of giving advice.
people.want: To stand in the hall at Hleidr once more and hear the last question asked, the one he was set there as a young man and could not answer.
people.fear: To die among Christians unable to speak, be signed with their cross and put in their ground.
people.voice: Short sentences with a picture in them; never says where he is from, and turns the question into a riddle.
people.looks: About forty-five, lean, weathered, fair hair gone grey and tied back, a short beard; a plain dark wool tunic and sea cloak, a knife and a whetstone at his belt, a small leather bag of rune-cut sticks.
knows: the hall riddles of the north, and who else carries them
the weather a day ahead, better than he admits
which men on the bank deal in people, and that he will not sit with them
Danish and Norse harbours: who is king there this year

lines.greet: You are late. The tide is not. I have a question for you when the cargo is aboard: an old one, the first one.
lines.greet_again: The boat is dry and the rope is new. That is all the news a boat has.
lines.greet_friend: Sit. I have kept the end of the bench and the end of the ale. Take one.
rumour: A man from Ripa says the king of the Danes is building again. He did not say what. Kings do not build barns.
The priest looked at me today as a cook looks at a goose. I shall drink on the far side of the fire.
Wind in the north-west by morning. The rooks at the graves told me, and my knee agreed with them.
lines.riddle: Would you have today what you had yesterday? Men have wanted that since the first hall. Tell me what it is.
lines.saying: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self. A good name does not. That is all the silver I trust.
lines.farewell: Go to your count. I will watch the boat. Nobody steals from a man who is looking at them.

people.name: Folcbert
people.trait: A soldier who holds a court because the king says so: fair by his own lights, bored by merchants, away with the host most summers.
people.want: His silver back at Michaelmas, or something better than silver: a service, a rare thing for his table, a favour he can show the king.
people.fear: The king's envoys finding his toll short or his court bought.
people.voice: Brief and loud, a man used to being obeyed outdoors; calls every Frisian 'shipman'.
people.looks: Mid forties, thick-set, short brown hair and a long moustache in the Frankish way, a red cloak pinned on the right shoulder over a mail-worn tunic, leg bindings, a sword he never takes off.
knows: what you owe and when: 1,920 pennies at Michaelmas

lines.greet: Shipman. You have my boat under you and my silver in her. Michaelmas. Hartwin has the stick.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat, shipman? Good. A drowned man pays nobody.
lines.greet_friend: Shipman! Sit down. No, at this end. Tell me what the English are paying for wine; my steward only tells me what I owe.
rumour: The Saxons killed Count Theoderic's men on the Weser. The king has turned back from the Avars. There will be a levy; there is always a levy.
The king wants every measure in my district made the same. I have fought Saxons. I would rather fight Saxons.
The bishop says the fine for a brawl on his bank is his. The bank may be his. The brawl was mine.
lines.debt: I do not want your reasons. I want eight pounds, or something I can show the king that is better than eight pounds.
lines.saying: A Frisian will swear the river is dry while he stands in it. I believe the tally.

people.name: Hartwin
people.trait: The count's steward: remembers every debt in the district and cuts each on a split tally stick; honest, and proud of being hard to cheat.
people.want: The tally to close clean on the day; failing that, a pledge he can hold in his hand.
people.fear: Being blamed for his lord's shortfalls; fire in the hall where the tallies hang.
people.voice: Counts aloud, in dozens and scores; never raises his voice.
people.looks: Past fifty, thin, grey, clean-shaven, a plain brown cloak with a bronze pin, a bundle of notched sticks at his belt and a small pair of scales in a box.

lines.greet: Your stick. Twenty score and four score pennies: four hundred and eighty. Here is your half. Do not lose it; I shall not lose mine.
lines.greet_again: Since you were last here: nothing paid, nothing added. The stick is as it was.
lines.greet_friend: Come in out of the wind. I have counted your stick twice this week for the pleasure of it. It is going down.
rumour: From the harvest on, every sack is measured by the king's new measure. Bring yours. If it is small I break it, and you thank me.
The king's price: wheat four pennies the measure, rye three, barley two, oats one. I did not make it. I only count it.
My lord rides with the host after Pentecost. Until he is back, what you say to me you have said to him.
lines.debt: Coin, or goods he will take, or a service. Three roads. I have cut a notch for each before; I will show you where.
lines.saying: A man's word and his half of the stick should fit. When they do not, I keep the stick.
lines.farewell: Michaelmas. I shall be here. I am always here.

people.name: Thiadbod

people.looks: About forty, well fed, combed fair beard, a long blue cloak of the best Frisian cloth with a silver pin, rings on two fingers, soft boots that have never hauled a boat.

the one toll man on the coast who weighs a gift and sends it up the river with the tally

gave the toll man on the Scheldt a good cloak one Easter and has been counted lightly since
wants the comb maker's whole summer at a price for the lot; the man will not sell that way

lines.greet: Neighbour! So that is the boat. She is a pretty thing. I had one like her when I was a boy.
lines.greet_again: Back already? I always say the short voyages are the safe ones. Wine at Lundenwic was eighty, when I left.
lines.greet_friend: Come aboard and drink something that was not brewed in a ditch. We are the only two on this river who can count.
rumour: The king's order shuts the English ports to Franks. I am a Frisian. I find the reeve at Lundenwic understands the difference, for a consideration.
Grain will be dearer by Candlemas. I say so as a friend. I would not sell yet, if I had any.
Your count is a fair man and a busy one. A debt is a weight to such a man. Somebody might take it off his hands.
lines.debt: Four hundred and eighty is nothing between neighbours. Let me carry it. You would hardly know I was there.
lines.saying: Give the toll man a cheese, the steward a hearing and the count a hawk. Nobody was ever searched by a friend.
lines.farewell: Fair wind, neighbour. Tell me what you see out there. I am always glad of news.

people.source: invented: the spine's cast.thiadbod, the rival Frisian skipper (Thiad- as in Thiadgrim, Liudger's father; -bod as in Radbod). The English ban: the quarrel of Charles and Offa, c. 790 to 796

people.name: Thiadburg
people.trait: Keeps the storehouse on the dam her husband built with what one ship brought away from York; lends on goods, forgets nothing, gives to the church without saying so.
people.want: The blood-price her husband Radger owed at Eoforwic paid before she dies, so her son can trade there; she will back a skipper who takes it.
people.fear: That her brother Thiadbod will have the storehouse when she is dead.
people.voice: Plain, quick, a little amused; asks what a thing weighs before she asks what it cost.
people.looks: A little over forty, upright, a white linen head-cloth, a dark gown with two round brooches and a string of amber and glass beads, a ring of keys at her belt.
knows: what lies in every storehouse on the dams, and whose it is
the story of York in 773, from the one who washed the blood out of the shirt
what she will lend on wine, cloth and stones, and for how long
her brother

ties.note: the same person
her younger brother, and her rival for the dam head
your steersman was her husband's ship's boy, and still does her errands unasked
her dead husband killed his brother in a brawl at York in 773; the wergild was never paid
her sacks reach the church door before light, and the priest does not say whose they are
the one officer she does not count twice after
her brother's boy, born in 787; she watches to see which of them he takes after
the old prior knows whose alms come by other hands, and says nothing, which she values
sends malt down the river on credit to the pilot's daughter, who has never missed a Michaelmas
sells her barley in thin years; she pays on the day
her boats sleep at Meinburg's house on the way north; two widows who lend on goods
has bought the terp's cloth for twenty years, and has never been late with the silver
two widows who do their own counting; word goes between them by every boat
