takes her best cloth when a boat is going south
buys her blue cloth, and sends word of prices
her cloth is stored at his house on the Strand by the season; she has never been cheated there
buys her cloaks by the score, and tried to beat her down once
her seller of twenty years at Cologne; they have met twice and trust each other's tallies
keeps his finished querns in her storehouse and has never shorted him a handful
his casks lie in her storehouse between the river boats and the sea boats (?)
bought the woman's cord one year and sent word that it held
her husband's host at York; she does not know he sold the four casks and kept the silver aside for her
her husband stood surety for his first cellar; a cask comes down from him each Martinmas
a cousin on her mother's side who went east and never sent word; she has had Masses said for him
a farm widow among the Svear who asks every southern skipper for cloth from this storehouse by name; they have never met

lines.greet: So you are the one with the count's boat. What does she carry? No, in weight. Everybody tells me what things cost.
lines.greet_again: Your corner is dry and your seals are whole. I looked this morning. I look every morning.
lines.greet_friend: Come in, mind the cat. I kept the high shelf for you; the river was in the low one at Candlemas.
rumour: My brother has grain in his house and is waiting for the price. I sold mine at the king's price. You may tell him I said so.
A storehouse is only a boat that stays. It leaks the same, and men who would not rob a ship will rob it.
Ask your steersman why he will not sail to York. Then come back, and I will tell you the part he leaves out.
lines.york: My husband killed a boy at York and ran. This house stands on what the ship carried home. I want it paid before I die.
lines.saying: Lend on the goods, never on the man. Goods do not have brothers.
lines.farewell: Go on. Bring me back something heavy.

people.source: invented: the spine's cast.thiadburg. Her husband is the 'certain Frisian merchant' of Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12, whom the source does not name; the name Radger is the spine's

people.name: Sigimar
people.trait: The moneyer of the king's mint: exact, incurious about people, curious about every coin; the first man on the Rhine to puzzle at a dirham.
people.want: Old pennies and foreign silver brought to him and not to the scales of a Dane; to know what the strange lettering says.
people.fear: A light coin with his mint's name on it; the king's law of 794 and the men who enforce it.
people.voice: Says a weight, then a loss, then nothing; warms only to a coin he has not seen before.
people.looks: About forty, stooped, burn-scarred forearms, a leather apron, a cap, a touchstone on a cord round his neck; behind him the anvil, the dies and a guard.
knows: what any silver is worth in the fire, to the grain
the day the old penny stops passing, before the toll man knows it
where foreign coin on the river comes from, by its look
a Latin riddle his clerk sells, about what money was before it was money

ties.note: the same person
they check each other's weights
the toll man takes coin by the look, the moneyer by the weight, and each thinks the other lazy
the Svea weighs silver the moneyer says must be struck
a brooch-maker who would rather keep old silver and look at it; a moneyer melts
his grandson, born in 798, who got the touchstone when he was nine
an English moneyer who says his pot takes a tenth and calls it the king's
let the bead man of the terps have glass on trust, and has been paid half
the clerk at Cologne and he send each other bad pennies as other men send greetings
compares weights with the Mainz moneyer by letter and by skipper; each takes the other's word on a coin
each says the other's pennies run light, and keeps one in a pouch to prove it
an old reciter among the Danes, never met: a rune-cut stick came to the mint by a Danish skipper, and an answer went back (?)
one of King Offa's moneyers, never met, who puts his own name on every penny: Sigimar melts them by the hundred and has not yet found a light one

lines.greet: Put it on the pan. All of it. I do not talk to silver in a purse.
lines.greet_again: You. Old pennies, Offa's, or broken? Say which, and I will say the loss.
lines.greet_friend: Ah. Come round the bench. I kept one for you to see: no cross, no king, only writing, like worms on a wet road.
rumour: The new penny is heavier by a third. Twelve to the shilling as before. The king has made every debt in the realm heavier and called it order.
From midsummer the old pennies go into my fire, less my cut. The toll man will refuse them. Do not try him; he enjoys it.
On the Frisian coast they still count by the light weight. I did not tell you that. A moneyer does not say such things.
lines.dirham: Where did this come from? Further than Rome? It is good silver. Better than mine. Do not tell anyone I said so.
lines.saying: A king's face on a coin tells you who to blame. The scale tells you the rest.
lines.farewell: Count it before you go out of the door. After the door it is your counting against mine.

people.source: invented: the spine's cast.sigimar. Carolingian pennies name the mint, never the moneyer. The light penny of 1.3 g and the monogram penny of 1.7 g, compulsory from 794; the coast kept the light weight (http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/B5.html)

people.name: Aldgrim
people.trait: The king's toll man on the dams for twenty years: dry, exact, impossible to hurry; remembers every hull and what she carried last time.
people.want: A quiet day, a full tally, and to hand the post to his sister's son and not to a Frank.
people.fear: The king's envoys counting behind him; a skipper who has cheated him once telling the others how.
people.voice: Says the hard thing first and plainly; the joke is that it is true.
people.looks: About forty-five, heavy, grey beard cut short, a plain brown cloak with a bronze pin worn short in the Frisian way, a tally stick in his belt, a cask-tapping mallet in his hand.
knows: who is in harbour, what they brought and what they paid on it
the tenth, the bank due and the 'giscot', and who is free of them: Saint Martin's men, and one abbey's ships
what the king forbids to go out: mail, and from 805 arms to the east
which casks ring wrong

ties.note: his sister; he eats at her house and pays, which she says is the only toll he ever paid
answers to the count for the king's tenth
has tapped his casks for ten years and never found anything, and does not believe it
each thinks the other has the easy half of the king's silver
the bishop's tenth of the king's tenth comes out of his tally, and the bishop's clerk counts it again
skippers tell her on the island what they did not tell him on the dam
once took the tenth on the ferryman's own supper, and would again
the reeve at Gipeswic: they have never met, and send each other the names of men who do not pay
a toll man on the Seine, known to him by the merchants who complain of both
the abbey's cellarer whose traders show a charter here every summer; he has tried to read it upside down

lines.greet: A tenth to the king. The rest is yours, if the river lets you keep it.
lines.greet_again: The small boat. Last time wine, six casks, and you counted five. Let us both count today.
lines.greet_friend: It is you. Stand in the shade; I will do the Frank in front first and take my time over him.
rumour: The king has shut his ports to the English. Whether a Frisian is a Frank is being argued on every dam. I say: ask the reeve at Lundenwic.
Stones for the English lie three deep on the bank and nobody buys. If I were young and owed money, I would think about that.
Saint Martin's men pay me nothing. They pay the saint. I have never met a saint who gave change.
lines.search: I am going to tap your casks now. It is nothing against you. I tap everybody's. Wine does not ring.
lines.saying: A short cloak for the long price. The king complained of ours. He still bought them.
lines.farewell: Go on. I have written you down. I write everybody down.

people.source: invented; the office from the charters of 777 and 815 (the king's 'procuratores rei publicae') and the precept of 828. The greeting is the spine's tone line for a Frisian toll man. The short cloaks: Notker I.34

people.name: Alfward
people.trait: Priest of the upper church, schooled at Utrecht: kind, overworked, short of everything; reads Latin slowly aloud and is ashamed that he does.
people.want: Bread for the people along his wall; a book carried safe to Utrecht; one day, a bell.
people.fear: A hungry winter with nothing to give; the heathen who took Lindisfarne finding the mouth of the Rhine.
people.voice: Gentle, tired, with a schoolboy's Latin tag now and then that he at once puts into plain words.
people.looks: Mid thirties, thin, tonsured, a patched grey-brown tunic and a short cloak, wooden shoes, ink on his right thumb, a small wooden cross and a letter in a leather case under his arm.
knows: the letter from York about the holy island, and what the bishop there will pay to have his people back
who on the bank is hungry and who is hoarding
what a book is, to a man who has never owned one
the feasts and fasts, and which days a ship should not be loaded

ties.note: his bishop; the church is Saint Martin's of Utrecht's since 777
the monk of York who brings him letters and a week of talk about books
Liudger taught him his letters at Utrecht, and he has never got over it
knows whose sacks come to the door before light
would like to baptise him, and has the sense not to say so twice a week
the count's men fine on the church's bank; the bishop writes; the priest carries the letters
she sends him the end of the pot and says it would only spoil; he blesses the pot
at school with him at Utrecht; they share one complaint about roofs
sells the church wax by a weight of his own; the priest buys elsewhere when he can

lines.greet: God keep you. You are the skipper with the new boat? I have a letter from York, thirteen days old, and I wish I had not read it.
lines.greet_again: You are back, and whole. Deo gratias. I mean: I am glad. Have you eaten? No, do not answer; nobody here has.
lines.greet_friend: Come and sit by the door, it is the only warm stone I have. Tell me where you have been. I never go further than Utrecht.
rumour: The heathen came to Saint Cuthbert's island on the sixth day before the ides of June. They killed brothers at the altar and took boys away in the ships.
There are forty along my wall today. Yesterday thirty. If you have grain, I will not ask what you paid for it.
I have a book that must go to the bishop at Utrecht. It is one day down the river. I would trust a careful man with it.
lines.leaf: A man back from Ripa showed me a leaf of a psalter. He bought it for a string of beads. He thought it was a pattern for weaving.
lines.saying: The saint cut his cloak in two for a beggar. I notice he kept half. I take comfort in that.
lines.farewell: Go with God. And if you pass Utrecht, tell them I am still here.

people.source: invented. The Upkirika and its tie to Utrecht: OSU 48 (777). The raid on Lindisfarne, 8 June 793, was thirteen days old on the game's first day; Alcuin's letters (texts_793.json alcuin_793). No priest of Dorestad is named in any source

people.name: Aldswith
people.trait: Keeps the house where shipmen lodge: brews, feeds, hears everything, repeats half; knows every crew on the river by its debts.
people.want: Her benches full and her roof whole; your crew paid before they drink; a husband for her niece who is not a sailor.
people.fear: Fire; a knife fight under her roof that brings the count's men in; being held to answer for a guest.
people.voice: Loud, quick and fond; calls every skipper 'son' and every skipper's debt by its exact sum.
people.looks: Near forty, broad, red forearms, a linen head-cloth, a wool apron-dress pinned with two plain bronze brooches, a ladle in her hand and a ring of keys on a cord.
knows: who came in today and from where, before the toll man does
which men want a berth and which should not be given one
what was said on her benches last night, in four tongues
what a bed, a meal and stabling cost, and who still owes her for them

ties.note: her brother the toll man eats here every evening and complains of the ale
the Northman has his own place by the door post and has never broken a pot
his men drink on credit and he pays late and smiling
sends the priest the end of the pot, and tells him it would only spoil
the Maas pilot sleeps here when he brings a ship up, and tells her how the channel lies
he drinks his day's pay slowly at her fire and has never broken a bench
the merchant who lodges nobody; she takes in the crews he turns away, and their pennies
the ale-wife at Gipeswic; they trade recipes and warnings about skippers by every boat
an ale-wife on the Seine she has never met; greetings and warnings go by the wine boats
her son's daughter, born the year before she died: the house, the brooches and the ladle go to her in the end

lines.greet: In you come, son, mind the dog. Ale is a farthing's worth the pot and the bed is by the wall. You are the count's four-eighty, yes?
lines.greet_again: There he is. Your Northman has been holding the door post up since noon. Sit; I will bring bread.
lines.greet_friend: Son! I kept the bench by the fire and told two Franks it was wet. What have you brought me from the sea?
rumour: A crew in from Lundenwic last night. The reeve turned them off the Strand with the wine still aboard. They drank a good deal of it here.
Thiadbod's steersman says they sail at the new moon for Ripa, wine in the casks. He said 'wine' twice. Men do not say it twice.
There is a Saxon asking for a berth, strong, no questions. I would ask him one or two, son, before the count's men do.
lines.crew: Three men want a berth this week. One is good, one is thirsty and one is my cousin. I will tell you which is which for a pot.
lines.saying: The black merchant shut his door on a poet, and the poet wrote it down. I let everybody in. Nobody has written about me.
lines.farewell: Pay your men before you pay me, son. Then pay me.

people.source: invented. A lodging at Dorestad: Rimbert c. 20; 'giscot', read as the shippers' payment for lodging (OSU 56; H6.html). The black merchant is Alcuin's Hrotberct (carmen 4). A host answers for a guest: the Kentish law of Hlothhere and Eadric c. 15, used here by likeness (?). 'A farthing' is a quarter of a penny by cutting (?)

people.name: Gerbrand
people.trait: The wright on the breaking beach: slow to speak, quick with an adze, judges a man by how he treats a boat he does not own.
people.want: Good oak from up the river, paid for before it is cut; one ship in his life built his own way from the keel.
people.fear: Green timber; a hull of his opening at sea with his mark on her stem.
people.voice: Talks about boats as 'she' and about owners as 'they'; answers a question with what it will cost.
people.looks: Early thirties in 793, grey by the end; short, thick wrists, sawdust in a brown beard, a leather apron over a short tunic, an adze over his shoulder and a bag of rivets at his belt.
knows: your boat better than you do: she is Norse-built, and he says so with respect
what a repair will cost, in pennies and in days
where oak, iron and sailcloth are to be had: Cologne, Deventer, the terps
which hulls in harbour are sound and which are for sale

ties.note: mends the big ship every spring and is paid at Michaelmas, sometimes the next one
the Northman knows how the boat was built and they talk about it in very few words
drinks his day's pay slowly at her fire
the Saxon in your crew has hauled timber for him

lines.greet: So this is her. Riveted, wool in the seams. Northmen built her. She is better than they told you and smaller than you think.
lines.greet_again: Haul her up and let me look under her. They always say she is dry. She is never dry.
lines.greet_friend: Leave her with me a week. I will do the garboard as well and not put it on the stick.
rumour: Oak is coming down from Cologne at the next high water. If you want a plank from it, say so before Thiadbod's man does.
The river is further from the dams than when my father worked here. Every few years they build the heads out. One day they will stop.
A sea-going ship takes me a winter and takes you a thousand pennies and more. Come back when you have a quarter of it.
lines.boat: She will carry what four men can load in a morning. Ask more of her and she will ask it back off the Maas mouth.
lines.saying: The sea finds the rivet you saved.
lines.farewell: Keep her bailed. And do not let them drag her over stones.

people.source: invented; the wright of the chain harbour.chain_house_new_ship (unnamed there). The beach finds and the Norse-built keel ship with wool caulking: Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md and Design/content/ships.md

people.name: Thiadlef
people.trait: Thiadbod's son and heir: his father's dam head and his father's smile, with less patience behind it; has buried silver twice and dug it up once.
people.want: To keep what his father built through the raid years, by paying whoever holds the river.
people.fear: Sails from the north at Pentecost; your house remembering what his father did to it.
people.voice: Smooth like his father until the Danes are mentioned; then short.
people.looks: About forty in the 820s, grey and thick by the 840s; a long blue cloak like his father's gone a little shabby, one ring, a short sword he has taken to wearing on the dam.
knows: what the last fleet took and what it left
who has silver in the ground, though not where
whom to pay among the Danes, and how much
what his father did about your house's debt, as his father told it

ties.note: his father, whose dam head and whose quarrels he inherited
his aunt; her son holds the storehouse he thinks should be his
paid the Danes when they held the place in Louis's time, and his sons pay them again
his sons pay Rorik's toll man well and are searched seldom
they have both buried silver, and compared how deep
the host on the Strand who keeps him the same bed in the raid years

lines.greet: You are of the house with the small boat. My father spoke of yours. He spoke of everybody. Come aboard.
lines.greet_again: Still trading? Good. There are fewer of us every Lammas.
lines.greet_friend: Our fathers would have laughed to see us share a cask. Let them. They are not paying for it.
rumour: They came by Utrecht, before anyone could ride ahead of them. The emperor was at Nijmegen by the time they had gone. He blamed us.
I do not keep silver in the house now. I keep it where a spade can find it and a Dane cannot.
The king has given the river to a Dane to keep the Danes off. It is a strange cure. I have paid for worse.
lines.saying: My father said: never break a law where you can be seen. I say: find out first whose law it is this year.
lines.farewell: If you see sails from the north, do not come and tell me. Run. I will see them soon enough.

people.source: invented: Thiadbod's son, named in Design/content/chains/house_rival.md (the fixed skipper of Dorestad after 825). The raids: Annales Bertiniani 834-837; Louis blaming disobedience, 837

people.name: Rorik
people.trait: A sea-raider made a count: keeps his oath for as long as it keeps him, and keeps other raiders off the river better than the emperor could.
people.want: The tolls of Dorestad, and a kingdom in Denmark if one comes loose.
people.fear: A stronger fleet than his own; the Frisians who drive him out in 867.
people.voice: Courteous Frankish with a Danish turn; bargains like a merchant and remembers like a king.
people.looks: About forty when granted the town: tall, fair, a moustache, a Frankish count's cloak and sword-belt over a northern tunic, gold arm rings, a ship's prow behind him; a cross on his breast by the 860s.
knows: which fleets are on the coast this summer, and whose they are
what the king's dues come to: he pays them in, less what he calls his trouble
Denmark: who is king, and how long he is likely to be
your house, if it has paid his toll without complaint

ties.note: the same person
his man at the toll
king of the Danes, whose kingdom he tries for in 855 and 857
the house that pays first and asks nothing
the old canon prays for his soul aloud; Rorik finds it presumptuous
an elder kinsman (?) who took baptism and the emperor's pay, and died for both
his brother (?), with whom he held Dorestad under the old emperor
held Dorestad of the old emperor with his brother, before the sons fell out (?)
a Dorestad man who paid his toll thirteen years, and thinks himself owed a river for it
one of his following, set to take the tenth on a Frisian stream (?)
a terp that pays his men when they can reach it, and calls it nothing
a Dane who farms among the Frisians and sends him nothing
the bishop who counts his absences aloud, and claims a tenth of his toll
the moneyer strikes the emperor's name and answers to him; Rorik leaves the mint alone so long as the dues come
one of the men of Oostergo who drove him out in 867 (?)
an ale-wife on the Scheldt who will not have his name said at her fire; his skippers drink there all the same
the archbishop calls him a wolf set to keep the fold; he has heard it and keeps the fold
the bishops of the eastern kingdom say he guards the river mouths for his cousins; he lets them say it
a wine merchant of the Seine who once passed Dorestad without paying and has been meaning to settle; Rorik remembers the ship
the king's man at Quentovic is set there to prevent Danes like him holding Frankish ports
a priest at Ripa who does not trust a baptised sea-king, and says so only in Latin
the ealdorman in Kent wants to know which ships off his coast are Dorestad's; Rorik does not help him
takes his due on the man's wine as it comes down through Dorestad, and lets it pass north unbroached
gives the bishop his peace when he travels by the Rhine mouth; it costs nothing and is remembered
the king of the Danes sits where Rorik's kin sat; in 855 Rorik goes home to try for it, and comes back

lines.greet: A merchant of the place. Good. I am the count now. The toll is the same toll; only the hand is different.
lines.greet_again: You again, and still paying. I like a man I do not have to look for.
lines.greet_friend: Sit. You were here before me and you will be here after me, if the river allows. Tell me what the Frisians say of me.
rumour: There are ships on the Scheldt that are not mine. They will not come up this river while I am on it. The king pays me for that.
I am going north for a season. There is a kingdom there with too many kings. Keep your silver somewhere I would not look.
The king's bishops write to ask what I knew of the last fleet. I knew they would leave if I asked them. I asked.
lines.saying: The king gave me the river to keep wolves off the sheep. He did not ask what I was.
lines.farewell: Trade in peace. It is mine, so it is worth having.

people.source: Annales Bertiniani 850, 855, 863, 867, 870; Annales Fuldenses 850, 857 ('qui praeerat Dorestado'); Annales Xantenses 873. He held the vicus with his brother Harald under Louis, took it in 850, and is dead by 882. His birth year, his words and his looks are ours (?); his baptism rests on Hincmar's letters, unread (?)

people.name: Eystein
people.trait: A Dane taking a Frankish king's toll for a Danish lord: exact, a little ashamed of the work, proud of keeping other pirates off the river.
people.want: The toll full, so that his lord keeps his grant; a Frisian wife and a house that does not burn.
people.fear: The next fleet being bigger than his lord's; being left behind when Rorik sails.
people.voice: Frisian with Danish bones in it; says 'the king's tenth' and means two kings.
people.looks: Mid thirties, fair, a moustache, a Frankish cloak over a northern tunic, an arm ring beside a toll man's tally stick; he may wear a small cross for the day's business.
knows: who paid and who went round by the Waal
when his lord is away, though he will not say it to a stranger
what northern buyers want from the Rhine this year: wine, glass, blades
the day of your reckoning: the debt is Rorik's now, and he keeps the stick

ties.note: the same person
his lord
Thiadbod's grandsons pay him well
the bishop of Utrecht still claims his tenth of the tenth, from a man who does not go to his church
listens to the old canon from the back of the church, and tells nobody in the hall
the island salter sends salt and word up the river
learned in his hall on the island how a Dane takes a Frankish king's dues
took his toll and, in the end, his jetty; they parted without a word
they came over in the same ship, and compare weights by the Almere boats
the moneyer says a penny is counted; the Dane at the toll weighs it all the same
buys Irish cloaks from the dealer at the black pool and asks no questions about the hands that wove them
takes the Seine man's wine at the toll and pays in good silver; no blessing is asked or given
sends word north to the priest at Ripa of which ships carry Christians
trades names of the taken with the clerk at Rotomagus, by any ship that will carry a strip of parchment
passes the man's casks at the toll and sends him the river's news
drinks at the old house on the bank road and pays, which surprises them both

lines.greet: The king's tenth. Yes, I know what I am. Put it on the stick; I count the same as the last man.
lines.greet_again: You paid last time without a speech. I remember the ones who do not make a speech.
lines.greet_friend: Friend. Lie at the near dam, the far ones are mud now. I will tell the boys you are not to be looked at.
rumour: No fleet has come up this river since my lord took it. Say that on the dams, when they call us wolves.
My lord sails north after the feast. When he is away I count the ships at the river mouth twice a day.
A woman from Birka is on the bank giving silver to the poor. From Birka. I did not know they had poor there to practise on.
lines.saying: A wolf at the door keeps the other wolves out. Feed him, and count your sheep at night all the same.
lines.farewell: Go on. If you meet ships like mine out there, they are not mine.

people.source: invented: the spine's cast.eystein. Rorik was to handle the king's dues and hold off the Danish pirates (Annales Fuldenses 850). The woman from Birka is Catla (Rimbert c. 20). Bishop Hunger of Utrecht, 854/56 to 866, fled the Northmen

people.name: Hrotberct
people.trait: The black-haired merchant of the bank: rich, close, quick with a price, and famous on the river for never having lodged a guest.
people.want: To sell wax to the churches at forty and buy it at twenty-five; and to be left out of poems.
people.fear: A buyer who weighs; the prior at Traiectum, who does.
people.voice: Fast and aggrieved: every price he names is robbing him, and he says so before you can.
people.looks: About fifty, lean, black hair going grey at the temples, a sharp shaved chin, a good dark tunic with no ornament at all, a covered balance always under his hand.
knows: what wax, honey and pepper fetch at every church between Colonia and the coast
every hull on the bank and whose debt she is
which toll men weigh and which only look
that a poet once put him in a letter, and what the letter says

ties.note: the old prior weighs his wax on the church's own scale, and tells every guest what it lacked
the poet he would not lodge, who paid him back in verse that the whole river can recite
Thiadbod gives where Hrotberct keeps; each thinks the other a fool with silver
the priest of the upper church buys his wax elsewhere when he can, and has said why from the door
she lodges the crews he will not, and takes their pennies for it

lines.greet: A small boat. Small boats want credit. I do not give credit, I do not give lodging, and I do not give advice. Wax, I sell.
lines.greet_again: You again. Did the cakes weigh what I said? Then somebody has been filing your weights.
rumour: The church at Traiectum wants wax before Candlemas and will pay forty. I know because I am the one it will pay.
Thiadbod gave the count a hawk. A hawk! I gave the count his toll, in full, on the day. Ask him which he remembers.
They say I turned a poet from my door. He had a boy with him and a horse. Do you know what a horse eats?
lines.saying: A guest is a debt that walks in by itself.
lines.farewell: Count it outside. I do not like counting in my shop; it makes people look at the scale.

people.source: historical in name only: 'niger Hrotberct', the 'mercator avarus' of Dorestad who will give the traveller no lodging, in Alcuin's carmen 4, lines 9-11 (MGH Poetae I, pp. 220-223), written before 782. That he was alive in 793, that he sold wax, and everything he says are invented (?).

people.name: Sigibald
people.trait: Sigimar's grandson at the same bench: as exact as the old man and less sure of anything, since he has struck three emperors' names and a Dane takes the toll.
people.want: Silver brought to the fire and not carried north to a scale; one year in which the die is not changed.
people.fear: The mint closed and the dies sent up the river; pennies with his town's name on them that he never struck.
people.voice: Says the weight and the loss, as his grandfather did, then adds 'for now'.
people.looks: A thin man in his thirties, later grey, with the family stoop and burn-scarred forearms, a leather apron, his grandfather's touchstone on a cord round his neck.
knows: what any silver is worth in the fire
which pennies with the emperor Lothar's name were never struck at any mint of his
what Rorik's man takes at the toll, and in what coin
whose house has put its silver in the ground

ties.note: his grandfather, who put the touchstone round his neck when he was nine
the head of the old lords' terp sends worn pennies south to be weighed, and trusts the answer
the Dane at the toll weighs coin that the moneyer says should be counted
they have both buried silver, and compared how deep
strikes for the emperor and answers to the Dane who holds the place
the count on the island sends word up the river when a fleet has passed; by then the mint has usually heard it from the fleet
tells her which of the new pennies to refuse, and is fed for it

lines.greet: On the pan. My grandfather would not talk to silver in a purse and I see no reason to begin.
lines.greet_again: You. The same loss as last time. For now.
rumour: There are pennies about with the emperor Lothar's name on them that were never struck in any mint of his. Good silver. Somebody north of here has a die and a steady hand.
Rorik's man weighs at the toll. Weighs! A penny is a penny or the king is not a king. I say this quietly.
Three houses on this bank have put their silver in the ground since the last fleet. I know which, because they stopped bringing it to me.
lines.saying: My grandfather said the scale tells you the rest. He did not live to see what the rest would be.
lines.farewell: Count it before the door. After the door it is anybody's count.

people.source: invented: the heir of the spine's cast.sigimar, named in the story dorestad.heavy_penny ('Sigimar's heir') and asked for by wijnaldum.eilrad. The mint of Dorestad struck for Louis the Pious and Lothar I, and imitations of Lothar's Dorestad pennies were made in Frisia in the 840s-850s (Coupland, 'Dorestad in the ninth century: the numismatic evidence', 1988; the hoards of Tzummarum and Pingjum (?)).

people.name: Aldgard
people.trait: Aldswith's granddaughter, who keeps the old house on the bank road in the Dane's years: pours for four tongues, gives to the church without counting, and counts everything else.
people.want: The house full and unburned for one more year; the poor along the church wall fed before the guests.
people.fear: Sails at Pentecost; and the river drawing off from the dams until no ship can lie near her door.
people.voice: Her grandmother's 'son' for every skipper, said more quietly; tells one story the same way every time.
people.looks: About twenty-five in 850: strong, grey-eyed, a linen head-cloth, a dark apron-dress pinned with two old bronze brooches that were her grandmother's, a wine jug in her hand as often as an ale ladle.
knows: who on the bank is truly poor and who only says so
which crews pay Rorik's man and which go round by the Waal
what a bed and a meal cost, in good pennies and in the poor new ones
the story of the bag from Birka, which she saw set down empty

ties.note: her grandmother, whose house, brooches and way with a debt she has
walked the holy places with the woman from Birka, and poured the four pennies' worth of wine
the Dane at the toll drinks at her house and pays, which neither of them expected
the moneyer tells her which of the new pennies to refuse

lines.greet: In you come, son. Ale is what it was. The pennies are not; I look at each one now.
lines.greet_again: The same boat, and still afloat. That is news enough for one evening. Sit.
rumour: A woman from Birka gave silver along the church wall today until her arms shook. I walked with her. I have not walked so far since my wedding.
The Dane's man pays for his ale. My grandmother would have fallen off her stool.
The big ships lie on the sand now. The river is a ship's length further from my door than when I was a girl.
lines.saying: Four pennies buys wine enough for a party of tired women. I know. I poured it.
lines.farewell: Go on, son. If you see sails at Pentecost, come back the short way.

people.source: invented, to make real the woman of the easter egg at dorestad.lodging ('Aldswith's granddaughter will tell you so in the 850s, and that she poured it') and of the cards harbour.catlas_purse.dorestad and harbour.catlas_bag.dorestad. The devout women who led Catla round the holy places are Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20 (Robinson 1921); none is named. Name of two attested Frisian parts, Ald- and -gard.

stories.title: The letter from York
stories.summary: On the first day the news of Lindisfarne is thirteen days old and the priest of the upper church has it in a letter. He wants a book carried to Utrecht; a year later a leaf of a psalter turns up on the dams, bought at Ripa for a string of beads, and it can be followed home.
stories.picture: A thin priest in the door of a timber church holds an open letter; behind him the poor sit along the wall, and below, two rivers and a small boat.

beats.text: Alfward reads you the letter: heathen men at Saint Cuthbert's, brothers killed, boys carried off. He asks you to take a book to the bishop at Traiectum, one day down the river, and to keep it dry.
The bishop's clerk takes the book, counts its gatherings, and tells you what such a thing is worth and to whom. (Sets bk_carried; a scribe may teach bk_knows_worth.)

A Frisian back from Ripa sells beads, combs and one painted leaf of calfskin he took for a weaving pattern. Alfward knows it for a psalter leaf from an English book. The man remembers who sold it. (Sets lf_trail_north.)
A goldsmith at Ripa cut the gold off the cover and sold the leaves by the handful. He names the crew that brought the book, and the boy they kept because he could tally.
The bishop on the island will pay for the leaf, and far more for a name. (Sets lf_knows_boys, if you do not have it.)

The schoolmaster knows the hand of the leaf for Northumbrian by the red dots round the great letter. The school will give sixty pennies and a standing order for calfskin; or the leaf can go home to the island it was cut from. (Selling or giving it sets bk_parchment.)

endings.how: You bought the leaf and carried it to Lindisfarena.
endings.text: The leaf is sewn back into nothing: the book is gone. But the bishop has it laid on the altar, and your name is said there.
endings.reward: 120 d from the bishop; the deed carried_letters; the priest and the monk Sigewine count you a friend; the trail to the boy Tidwine

endings.how: You sold the leaf to the bishop at Traiectum.
endings.text: Hamacar pays a fair price and puts it in the school's chest, where boys copy its letters for sixty years.
endings.reward: 60 d; a standing order for calfskin from the school (bk_parchment); Alfward is disappointed in you and says nothing

endings.how: You kept the leaf, or let the Frisian sell it to a bead maker.
endings.text: It is cut into strips to bind amber. One strip with half a blue letter on it hangs in a workshop for a generation.
endings.reward: Nothing but the price of the beads; the trail north stays open if you asked the seller first

stories.reward: A friend at the church in every later year; the book road (bk_carried); the first step toward the boys of the holy island.

stories.title: What Radger owed
stories.summary: Thiadburg's storehouse stands on what one ship carried home from York in 773, when her husband killed a nobleman's son and every Frisian fled. She wants the blood-price paid before she dies; her brother would rather York stayed shut.
stories.picture: A widow with a ring of keys stands in the dark door of a storehouse on a dam; behind her shoulder, on a high shelf, a small iron-bound chest that is never opened.

beats.text: Thiadburg tells it plainly: the brawl, the dead boy, the ship loaded in the dark, your own steersman a child aboard her. She will put up a part of the price, and wants her son named in the settlement. (Sets yk_feud_known.)
Thiadbod has heard you were asking. He is sorry for his sister, and thinks old blood is best left to dry. He does not say that he trades at York himself, under an English name.
At York the dead youth's brother Ecgwulf learns whose ship you sail and who steers her. (Sets yk_named.) Before the archbishop's man he names a price. (Sets yk_price_set.)
She opens the chest on the high shelf. It holds less than the price. The rest is yours to find, or her brother's to offer, on terms.
The silver is weighed on the church's scales and Ecgwulf takes it, or does not. (Sets yk_paid.)
Aldger's mother unties a knotted cloth: twelve light pennies, his ship's boy's wage from the voyage that fled York. She means them to be laid down first.
The chest in the school holds the books Liudger carried home on that same ship. The schoolmaster, who stayed behind, tells it as a thing that happened to a friend.

endings.how: You carried the price to York with her share in it and had her son named.
endings.text: Eoforwic opens to Frisians for the first time in forty years. Thiadburg's son trades there; Aldger walks the strand under his own name. She dies knowing it.
endings.reward: Eoforwic open to the house (yk_paid); Thiadburg stands surety for your debt (db_surety); a corner of her storehouse free for your lifetime; her son a friend to your heir

endings.how: You paid it all yourself and left her son out.
endings.text: York opens, and the profit of it is yours alone. Thiadburg thanks you and counts her keys. Her son remembers who was first through the door.
endings.reward: Eoforwic open to the house (yk_paid) and a season there without a Frisian rival; her feeling cools; her son a rival to your heir

endings.how: You took Thiadbod's advice, or his silver, and let it lie.
endings.text: York stays shut. Thiadbod goes on trading there as an Englishman. Aldger never asks you again. When Thiadburg dies, her brother has the storehouse within the year.
endings.reward: 80 d from Thiadbod and week-old news from York each spring; Thiadburg will not lend again; the storehouse passes to your rival

stories.reward: Eoforwic, the richest market of the north, opened or lost; and the widow's surety against the count's day.

stories.title: The count's stick
stories.summary: The boat was bought on the count's silver: 1,920 pennies, due at Michaelmas, cut on a split stick that hangs in the hall at De Geer. It can be met with coin, with goods he will take, with a service, with the widow's surety, or it can pass into Thiadbod's hands.
stories.picture: A thin grey steward holds up one half of a split notched stick against the other half, in the door of a hall hung with hundreds of them.

beats.text: Hartwin gives you your half of the tally and shows you his: twenty-four score. The count calls you shipman and names the day.
Thiadbod offers, as a neighbour, to take the debt off the count's hands. (If he does: db_bought.)
Thiadburg lends on goods left under her seal, and will stand before the steward for a skipper she trusts. (Sets db_surety.)
The reckoning at Michaelmas: the king's new pennies, goods the count will take, or an errand in place of part of the silver. (A service sets db_service; a delay, once, db_extension.)
The count's errand: English hounds and a cloak of the old length. Other regions hold other errands for him.
A later generation's day: the debt is owed to the Dane who holds the toll, and Eystein keeps the stick. He counts the same as Hartwin did, and waits less.

beats.when: feast and year < 813 and debt > 0 and not flag.db_extension
beats.text: On a feast at the king's house the count sits among his equals. A gift carried in before them cannot be refused, and a delay asked for there is hard to deny. (Sets db_extension.)
The bishop, who disputes every fine with the count, will stand between the steward and a house that has carried for Saint Martin's. (Sets db_surety.)

endings.how: You paid in full in the new pennies on Michaelmas.
endings.text: Hartwin fits the two halves together, breaks them over his knee and gives you the pieces. The count remembers the name of one Frisian.
endings.reward: The boat is yours; the count's and the steward's feeling up; credit with the count for a bigger ship (the chain harbour.chain_house_new_ship)

endings.how: You met part of it with an errand or with goods the count wanted.
endings.text: The stick is cut down, not broken. You are the count's shipman now, which is a debt of another kind and a door of another kind.
endings.reward: The debt eased; an errand's pay; a place below the salt at the count's feast; the toll eased for a season

endings.how: You let the debt pass to Thiadbod.
endings.text: The count has his silver and has forgotten you. Thiadbod has your stick on his own wall, and is very friendly.
endings.reward: A year's delay and no interest named; Thiadbod chooses one cargo a year for you until it is paid (the chain's 'sold' road)

stories.reward: The house's freedom, or its first master: every later generation's day is measured against this one.

stories.title: The heavy penny
stories.summary: In the game's first year the king makes his penny heavier by a third, and from midsummer 794 the old ones go into the moneyer's fire at a loss. Sigimar is exact and dull until someone puts a coin on his pan that he cannot read.
stories.picture: A stooped man in a leather apron holds a small silver coin up to the light of a doorway, frowning at it; on the bench lie scales, dies and a heap of old pennies.

beats.text: Sigimar weighs your purse: light pennies with the axe, a few of Offa's, a cut sceat. He tells you the day the old coin stops passing, before it is cried on the dams.
The toll man refuses old pennies at their face. If you try him and he sees it, he remembers. (Sets sv_old_coin.)
On the Frisian coast they still count by the light weight: old pennies pass there that the mint would melt. The moneyer did not tell you this.
You show him a dirham from the north. He turns it for a long time, tests it, and says it is better silver than the king's. (Sets sv_first_dirham and sv_moneyer_trusts.)
Holmfast the Svea reads you what he can of it: not the words, but the weight, the nick and where it has been. He will not have it struck into pennies for any king.
Martinmas 825 is the last day for the old pennies. Sigimar's heir remembers whose house brought silver to the fire and whose took it to a Dane's scales.

endings.how: You brought him your foreign silver and the first dirham he ever saw.
endings.text: He takes your word on what a strange coin is, and his loss on your silver is the smallest on the river. He keeps the dirham in a pot by the dies and looks at it on feast days.
endings.reward: The mint's cut on your silver halved for life (sv_moneyer_trusts); a true word a week early whenever the coin changes; 40 d for the dirham

endings.how: You ran the old pennies north and learned the scale.
endings.text: You make a third on every old penny for two summers and can weigh hacked silver with any Dane. Sigimar knows what you did and tells the toll man.
endings.reward: About 150 d over two seasons; a folding scale and the northern weights (sv_scale); the moneyer and the toll man both cool

endings.how: You passed old coin at the toll and were seen.
endings.text: The pennies are taken, the fine is paid, and for a year every purse you open on the dams is weighed in front of you.
endings.reward: A fine of 60 d (the king's ban is sixty shillings for the stubborn; you are let off with pennies (?)); the lesson; the moneyer, oddly, thinks no worse of you

stories.reward: A moneyer who trusts your word, or a scale of your own: two ways of knowing what silver is.

stories.title: Stones on the dam
stories.summary: While the king's quarrel with Offa shuts the ports, quernstones finished here for the English trade pile up unsold and cheap, and English cloth is dear. On every dam they argue whether a Frisian is a Frank.
stories.picture: Grey lava quernstones stacked three deep along a dam like loaves, a quern cutter sitting idle on the pile, skippers arguing in the foreground.

beats.text: The quern cutter will sell finished stones at two thirds of last year's price to anyone who will take them off his bank. He says the English are grinding with their teeth by now.
Aldgrim tells you the order as it reached him: the king's ports are shut to the English, and theirs to us. Whether it binds Frisians he will not say. (Sets bs_ban_heard.)
The wic-reeve decides, for your boat and on that day, whether a Frisian is a Frank.

The first ship of the summer brings word of the king's letter to Offa: the stones may be of the length the English ask, and the cloaks of the old length. The price of querns here doubles in a week. (Sets bs_peace.)
On the Almere shore a stone-dresser has two summers' querns in the nettles, and curses a reeve he has never seen.
A skipper at Wiltrud's fire swears that Offa is dead and the ports will open by the next moon. He said so last Easter too. It is not true until the summer of 796.

endings.how: You bought stones cheap during the ban and held them, or got them across.
endings.text: When the peace comes your stones are already on the Strand, or already in the widow's store at the old price.
endings.reward: A good voyage's profit, 150 to 300 d; the quern cutter's standing order; a quern-dresser's shed on your plot becomes worth having

endings.how: You left the stones alone until the letter came.
endings.text: You pay the new price with everybody else, and sail in company, and are turned away by nobody.
endings.reward: An ordinary profit and no enemy at Lundenwic; the reeve has no mark against your name

stories.reward: The game's first lesson in old news: the price of a stone is the age of a letter.

stories.title: The king's measure
stories.summary: The first summer is a famine. Thiadbod has grain in store and waits for Candlemas; his sister sells hers at the king's price and says so. From the harvest of 794 the steward checks every measure against the new one.
stories.picture: A steward pours grain from a merchant's small wooden measure into a larger iron-bound one that it does not fill; thin people watch from the church wall behind.

beats.text: The poor sit along the church wall. Alfward does not ask what you paid for your grain. He asks whether you have any.
Wheat that cost six pennies the sack sells at twelve on the dams. Thiadbod's doors are shut and his men say the house is empty. Thiadburg's are open.

Hartwin checks your measure against the king's new one. If it is short he breaks it, and gives you leave to buy a true one. (Sets hy_new_measure.) The king's price is cried: wheat four pennies the measure.
The hunger comes again, and with it the king's order that no grain leave the realm. The same doors are shut, by the sons of the same men.
The old prior at Saint Martin's asks what rye costs on the dams at Dorestad, and waits. He has the king's order to feed the hungry and no grain to do it with. (A fair sale there sets hy_fed_poor.)
On the terps the king's price is hearsay and bread is paid for in cloth. What a boat charged at Dorestad is known here by the next boat.
Below the king's house forty people who belong to no lord sit by the old graves. The priest asks for nothing, and says how many they are.

beats.when: (year = 805 and month >= 10) or year = 806 or (year = 807 and month <= 8)
beats.text: At the last Frankish landing the king's price meets the Danes' price. Rye that may not lawfully leave the realm fetches nine pennies by weight over the side of a hull bound north.

endings.how: You sold or gave grain at or under the king's price.
endings.text: The church remembers. So does everybody along the wall, and they are the people who carry cargo and hear things.
endings.reward: The deed gave_alms or fair_dealing (hy_fed_poor); the priest a fast friend; porters work for you first; the bishop will hear a request

endings.how: You sold above the price and were seen.
endings.text: You made twice the silver in half the time. The steward has a notch for it, and the count's men may ask.
endings.reward: Double profit on the grain, 60 to 120 d (hy_sold_dear); the steward cool; a question from the king's men in a later year

stories.reward: Who stands with you on the bank in a bad year: the church and the poor, or nobody.

stories.title: Casks that ring
stories.summary: The king forbids mail and blades to leave the realm, and the toll man taps every cask. Thiadbod sends sword blades north in wine casks and has never been caught; he would be glad of a second, smaller boat that nobody looks at.
stories.picture: A heavy toll man bends with his ear to a wine cask on a dam, mallet raised; a well-dressed skipper watches from his ship, smiling, thumbs in his belt.

beats.text: Aldgrim, and after him every toll man, taps the casks and lifts the ballast boards. A man found with blades loses them and is written down. (Sets sw_marked.) A man who gets them past has sw_ran_blades, and a toll man who learns of it later remembers.
Thiadbod's steersman says 'wine' twice. Aldswith notices. So may you.
Thiadbod offers you a small cargo for the north, already casked and sealed, the toll already seen to. He names a buyer. (Sets sw_buyer_known.)
On the inland water north, out of the count's sight, a cargo changes boats at night.
A generation on, a man on the dams turns over a sword taken from a dead raider. The blade has a Rhine smith's mark, and a cask stain in the fuller.
At the last Frankish landing a ferryman takes twelve bundles into a north-bound hull at moonset, and names the man they are for. (Sets sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known.)

endings.how: You told Aldgrim which casks ring.
endings.text: For once he taps the right one. Thiadbod pays a fine that would buy your boat, smiles, and never forgives you.
endings.reward: The finder's share if the year allows it (from 806 half the goods (?)), or 100 d from the count; the toll eased for a year; Thiadbod's lasting enmity

endings.how: You carried the casks north.
endings.text: The blades sell for four times their price in the Rhineland. You know a buyer by name now, and he knows you.
endings.reward: 200 to 300 d; sw_ran_blades and sw_buyer_known; a hold over Thiadbod and his over you; the risk of sw_marked at every later search

endings.how: You said no and said nothing.
endings.text: Thiadbod is as friendly as ever and never offers again. Aldgrim taps your casks no less.
endings.reward: Nothing lost; Aldswith thinks better of you, and tells her brother so

stories.reward: Silver now, and a blade that may come back up the river in 834 in another man's hand.

stories.title: The first question
stories.summary: Ravn sets his first riddle at Dorestad, the oldest in the hall contest, and gives the next only when it is answered. A clerk at the mint sells a Latin one about money; a merchant's son schooled at Utrecht has one about the anchor.
stories.picture: Evening on a dam: a lean grey Northman sits on a mooring post holding up a rune-cut stick, a cup of ale untouched beside him.

beats.text: Ravn asks what a man had yesterday and wants today, that harms men, hinders words and yet rouses them. He will not help. (The riddle r-gest-01; answered, it gives the stanza of the names of ale, t-alv-34.)

The moneyer's clerk sells, for ten pennies, three lines of Latin about a thing that was earth and hid in earth, was given another name by fire, and now buys earth. (riddle_symphosius_91_pecunia; answered here, no king's toll on your sales at Dorestad for two years.)

A merchant's son home from the school at Utrecht sets a riddle over the ale about two iron points joined in one, that fights wind and deep water and bites the land itself. (riddle_symphosius_61_ancora; answered, the freshest word on prices here.)
A salter up from the coast has a Latin riddle a monk taught him about his own goods, and sells it with a sack. It is the first of a longer road. (riddle_aldhelm_19_salis.)
The men who pass you riddles in the north turn out to be Ravn's old hall-fellows. At Hleidr he tells you the question he could not answer. (Sets rd_last_question.)
The schoolmaster at Saint Martin's sets every new boy three lines about a thing that keeps the house for its master. He sets them to shipmen too. (riddle_symphosius_04_clavis.)
A palace clerk has the river and the fish on a wax tablet and nobody to try it on. (riddle_symphosius_12_flumen.)

endings.how: You answered Ravn, and the clerk, and the boy.
endings.text: Ravn nods once and gives you a stick with a stanza cut on it. Next morning he has another question ready. He has had it ready for years.
endings.reward: The text t-alv-34; toll freedom here for two years (rw_toll_dorestad); a price tip (rw_tip_dorestad); the deed won_riddle; Ravn's next riddle

endings.how: You let the question lie.
endings.text: Ravn says nothing more about it. He goes on doing his work well. Now and then he looks at your ale and then at you.
endings.reward: Nothing lost: the riddle waits, and wakes again whenever ale or mead is bought

stories.reward: The road of riddles opens: a stanza, two years without the king's tenth, and a teacher who has decided you are worth asking.

stories.title: The king's ships go overland
stories.summary: The count is away with the host most summers and his steward keeps the tally. In 797 the king has ships hauled by river and over land into Saxony, and boats and men on the Rhine are pressed for it.
stories.picture: Men and oxen haul a ship on rollers up a muddy bank under a grey sky; a count on horseback points with a sword still in its scabbard.

beats.text: The hall is half empty: the count rides with the host. Hartwin hears what you would have said to his lord, and is easier to find and harder to move.
The count's men walk the dams choosing boats and backs for the king's ships that are to go overland into Saxony. A small boat is easy to overlook, or easy to take.
On the IJssel, at the edge of Saxony, your mate Brunger asks every chained man that passes whether he has seen his brother. (Sets sx_brother_trail.)
A strong Saxon with no kin asks Aldswith for a berth and no questions. The king's men are asking for a man like him. (Carrying him sets sx_carried_fugitive.)

endings.how: You gave your boat and a month to the count's hauling.
endings.text: You come home thin, with a notch cut off the stick and a count who knows your face.
endings.reward: 60 to 120 d off the debt (db_service); the count's feeling up; Brunger has word of where the hostages went

endings.how: You were at sea when the count's men came, or took the Saxon out of their reach.
endings.text: Nobody says anything. Hartwin cuts a small mark on the back of your stick, where it does not count, yet.
endings.reward: A season's free trading; a strong hand at the oar who owes you his neck; the steward wary

stories.reward: The count's favour or a Saxon's loyalty: you cannot easily have both.

stories.title: Two hundred sails
stories.summary: In 810 Godfred's fleet comes down on Frisia and takes a hundred pounds of silver. The count calls out men and boats for the emperor's host, and everything an army eats goes up. Then word comes that Godfred is dead by his own man's hand.
stories.picture: A count's man with a spear walks down a dam counting boats on his fingers; skippers stand by their mooring ropes looking at the river mouth.

beats.text: Two hundred ships have landed in Frisia, the islands are burned, and the Frisians have paid a hundred pounds. Every boat here is counted for the host, and your share of the hundred pounds is asked.
Bread, salt pork, oats and ale go up by half while the emperor's host lies on the Weser. Whoever has them in store names his price.
A crew in from the coast says Godfred is dead, killed by one of his own following, and his nephew wants peace. Ravn puts down his cup and for once asks a plain question: which man.
On the Almere shore the row's share is weighed out in brooches and dowry strings, and comes up short by two hands of silver.
At the Ems mouth the free men stand in the ring while each household's share is told off. A Dorestad boat is asked for its part like anyone else. (Sets gf_paid_share.)

endings.how: You paid your share and sold food to the host at a fair price.
endings.text: The Danish ships let you be that season, and the count's quartermaster asks for you by name the next time.
endings.reward: gf_paid_share; 80 to 150 d from the host's buying; a standing order from the count's table

endings.how: You carried the warning to a Frisian port before the fleet came.
endings.text: A terp has its cattle and its children inland by the time the sails show. They do not forget which boat came in rowing.
endings.reward: gf_warned; fast friends at that port, and free lodging there for your lifetime

stories.reward: A name on the Frisian coast, in the one summer when the whole coast was afraid.

stories.title: The river leaves
stories.summary: From 834 a fleet comes up the river year after year: it burns, kills, carries people off and takes tribute. In 850 the king gives the place to a Dane to keep the others out. In January 863, with the rivers in flood, the last sack comes, and the river itself is already leaving the dams.
stories.picture: A winter flood at dusk: black water over the low ground, the roofs of storehouses standing out of it, and far down the river a line of long ships with their masts down.

beats.text: Word comes down the Crooked Rhine a day ahead of the ships: they are past Utrecht. Load and run up the Lek, put the silver in the ground, or stay with the storehouse. (Burying sets df_buried; bringing the word here yourself, df_warned.)
After each raid: church plate and Frankish cloth sold cheap by men who do not say where they got them; a widow selling a dam head; survivors asking after kin sold at Sliesthorp.
From the palace hill at Nijmegen the emperor Lothar watches the smoke of Dorestad and two other villages, and does nothing, because there is nothing he can do.
Rorik's man Eystein takes the tenth where Aldgrim's grandson took it. Pay and be known to him, or go round by the Waal. (Swearing to Rorik's peace sets df_rorik_man.)
The flood winter. The merchants flee to a large estate inland and are killed there. Rorik talks the fleet into leaving. Afterwards a priest asks you what you saw, and what Rorik knew.
The heirs of Thiadbod and Thiadburg sell their timber and choose a town. So must you. (Sets df_moved.)
New plots on the IJssel with old Dorestad names on them. The bishop's men there keep 'the freedom they had at Dorestad', and argue about what it was.
A canon of the old minster asks every skipper he trusts for one promise: a boat for the church's chest, if the bishop must go.
This year the Northmen burned Witla at the Maas mouth. The pilot's family took their marks elsewhere, and no fire was lit on the dune again.
The count of Walcheren has forty spears and an island with no wall. He asks a merchant to carry his word up the river, since the palace does not believe counts.

endings.how: You moved the house to Daventre, Traiectum or Tiel before the flood winter.
endings.text: The house has a new plot on a new river and the old stick of names. Its children say 'at Dorestad' the way other people say 'in the old king's day'.
endings.reward: df_moved; a plot in the new town at half its price (unlock_plot_daventre or the like); your Dorestad friends' heirs as neighbours; the buried silver, if you dug it up first

endings.how: You swore to Rorik's peace and stayed to the end.
endings.text: For twelve years it is the safest river in Frisia. Then it is not. You are among those who are warned in the flood winter, because the warning came from his side.
endings.reward: df_rorik_man; the toll eased while Rorik holds the town; your life in 863; a bishop's clerk with questions afterwards

endings.how: You neither paid the Dane nor left.
endings.text: The house loses its store in the last sack and the plot to the clay. What is in the ground is still in the ground, if anyone alive knows where.
endings.reward: The goods in store are lost; df_buried silver can still be fetched by you or an heir; the name of Dorestad's freedom, which is worth something at Tiel

stories.reward: The house outlives its town, with its silver, its friends or only its name.

stories.title: Catla's purse
stories.summary: In the 850s Catla of Birka comes with her dead mother's silver for the poor of Dorestad, because Birka has few poor and Dorestad has many. Devout women lead her round the holy places; when they are weary she spends four pennies on wine, and finds the bag full again, less the four.
stories.picture: A sunburned woman in a travelling cloak sits on a bench with a heavy leather bag on her lap, three older women beside her sharing a cup; a church door stands open behind.

beats.text: A ship from the north lands a Svea woman who carries her own bag and asks, in careful Frisian, for the women who know which of the poor are truly poor.
She gives at every holy place in turn, counting aloud. A skipper the bank trusts may be asked to walk beside her through the dams, where a bag like that is watched.
Half the silver is given. She and the women are tired, and she buys four pennies' worth of wine. At her lodging the bag is as heavy as when she came: full, but for the four pennies.
At Birka they ask what became of Frideburg's silver. A merchant who was there can tell it, and is believed or not according to his name.

endings.how: You walked beside her and carried word home to Birka.
endings.text: The priests she tells say the Lord repaid what was given, and kept back what was spent on wine. At Birka the Christians lodge you as kin.
endings.reward: The deed gave_alms; a welcome among Birka's Christians and free lodging there; the poor of the bank know your boat; a passage paid at 40 d

endings.how: You only sold her the wine.
endings.text: Four pennies, fairly earned. They are the only four she did not get back, and the story is told for two hundred years with your wine in it.
endings.reward: 4 d; and a thing to tell at any Christian table north of the Eider

stories.reward: A friend at Birka and a place in a story Rimbert wrote down.

works.name: A corner of the widow's storehouse
works.what: A dry corner under Thiadburg's roof, your goods under her seal with a tally stick tied on. She lends on what lies there.
works.needs: Thiadburg, or her heir, must know you.
works.gives: Goods kept ashore at Dorestad: buy when a thing is cheap and sell when it is dear. She will lend up to half their worth against the count's day.
works.picture: Sealed sacks and three casks in a dim corner of a timber storehouse, a tally stick tied to each, a cat asleep on a bale.
works.source: story/works_793.json store_corner (6 d a month); the large warehouses on the dams, c. 750-830 (Van Es and Verwers)

works.name: A plot on the bank
works.what: One of the long narrow plots that run from the bank road down to the river, eighteen paces wide, with the right to build a dam out from it as far as the water goes.
works.needs: The port must know your house; bought from the count's steward, or from a widow who is leaving.
works.gives: Ground of your own (unlock_plot_dorestad): a stock here, a winter berth, a roof for the crew, and the place a storehouse, a well and a dam can stand. Twelve pennies a year to the lord at Martinmas.
works.picture: A narrow strip of trodden ground between two wattle fences running down to brown water, four corner posts freshly driven and a steward pacing it out.
works.source: Hoogstraat: parcels 18 m wide with paired dams (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_plot_dorestad

works.name: Your own dam, built out to the water
works.what: An earth-and-wattle dam on rows of oak posts from your plot to the stream, with a plank way on top. The river draws away east a little every year, so it must be lengthened about every twelve years or it ends in mud.
works.needs: A plot on the bank; posts ordered from up the river; a summer when the comb stands dry.
works.gives: Your own berth at the head (unlock_work_dorestad_jetty): no waiting for a place, loading in half the time, a ship of any size can lie at it. Thirty pennies a year to keep.
works.picture: Men driving oak posts into a dry river bed in two rows, wattle hurdles and baskets of earth between, the water a long way off.
works.source: Dams 6 to 7 m wide and up to 200 m long, 10,000 posts to 100 m of bank, in use c. 675-875 (Van Es and Verwers; H8.html); BRIEF_2.md (600 d, 90 days)

works.name: A well lined with a wine cask
works.what: A shaft dug behind the house and lined with two or three old Rhenish casks with their ends knocked out, one on another.
works.needs: A plot on the bank, and two empty wine casks.
works.gives: Clean water for the crew and for brewing: provisioning here costs less, and sickness ashore is rarer. In a raid year, a place to drop a purse.
works.picture: A man stands waist deep in a hole lowering a bottomless wine cask into it; a second cask waits on the grass.
works.source: Some 650 wells lined with Rhenish wine casks of silver fir and oak, felled 685-835 (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md; story/works_793.json well)

works.name: A quern-dresser's shed
works.what: A lean-to on your plot where a cutter finishes lava stones that come down from Mayen as rough-outs: the eye bored, the faces dressed, the pair matched.
works.needs: A plot on the bank; a cutter from the row behind the bank road who will work for you.
works.gives: Rough-outs bought on the Rhine leave Dorestad as finished querns at a third more: the English and the Danes pay for the finishing.
works.picture: A man grey with stone dust sits astride a black lava disc under a lean-to, pecking its face with a pick; finished pairs are stacked behind him.
works.source: Mayen lava querns came as roughouts and were finished here (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md; story/works_793.json quern_shed) (?)

works.name: A house for the poor by the upper church
works.what: A timber house by Saint Martin's where the poor and strangers are given bread, ale and a place by a fire: what a rich man's alms became when he wished them to last.
works.needs: Promised before the priest of the upper church; the port must know your house.
works.gives: The poor of the bank know your boat (unlock_work_dorestad_hospice): word from the river mouth reaches you a day sooner. Your name is said at mass, and there is a grave for you by the church. Eighty pennies a year to keep.
works.picture: A new timber house beside a small church, its door open, a woman ladling from a pot to a line of thin people; fresh wood shavings on the ground.
works.source: 'A multitude of poor people' at Dorestad and Catla's alms: Rimbert c. 20 (Robinson 1921); story/unlocks_793.json. No such house is recorded here: it is ours (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand, or mended to as good as new
ships.note: Your own boat's kind: a small riveted clinker boat of northern build, such as Danes and Frisians bring up the river and sometimes sell on the beach. Gerbrand can mend one but would not build one: it is not his way of laying a plank.
ships.picture: A small open clinker boat with four oars and a short mast lying between two dams, her planks dark with tar.
ships.source: The Dorestad keel-ship fragment is Norse-built clinker with wool caulking, after c. 739 (Design/content/ships.md)

ships.note: The working boats of the dams: lighters, ferry boats, fishing boats with wicker cars. Boats of two to three metres' beam lay between the dams.
ships.picture: A blunt little plank boat poled along a ditch between two dams, a wicker fish car towing behind.
ships.source: Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md (boats of 2 to 3 m beam between the dams); H11.html (fish cars)

ships.how: bought second-hand, or hired by the day
ships.note: For errands across the river and up the ditches when the comb is half dry.
ships.picture: A flat punt with one man standing in the stern, poling across the brown river toward the far bank's willows.

ships.note: The old river freighter of this water, an oak log hewn and spread with planks added: slow, cheap, and good on the Crooked Rhine down to Utrecht and the Vecht.
ships.picture: A long narrow boat hewn from one great oak, with a plank added along each side, loaded with pots packed in straw.
ships.source: Design/content/ships.md (the forerunner of the Utrecht type)

ships.how: hired with her men, or bought second-hand
ships.note: The Rhine merchant's own freighter: wine and stones down from Cologne and Mainz, towed back up on a long rope. She cannot go to sea.
ships.picture: A long flat-bottomed barge stacked with wine casks, six men on the bank hauling her upstream on a rope.
ships.source: The Cothen barge in the old Rhine bed below Dorestad, after c. 826; Alcuin's tow-rope (carmen 4) (Design/content/ships.md)

ships.how: built to order over a winter on the breaking beach; after 834 bought second-hand from houses that are leaving
ships.note: The Dorestad merchant's ship, the one on the king's penny: for Lundenwic, Quentovic, Ripa and the Jutland coast. Gerbrand builds one in a winter if the oak is bought at Cologne, the iron at Deventer and the sailcloth on the terps.
ships.picture: A broad, high-ended ship with a single mast and a steering oar, drawn up on blocks on a sandy beach with her planking half done.
ships.source: The ship on the deniers of Dorestad, 812-818 (B5.html); Design/content/ships.md; the chain harbour.chain_house_new_ship

ships.note: While a Dane holds the town, a northern ship that rows as well as she sails can be had from a man going home, for silver by weight. She needs twelve men.
ships.picture: A long low northern ship with a row of oar ports and a striped sail, moored at a dam head with shields stacked amidships.
ships.source: Rorik's Danes at Dorestad, 850-867 (Annales Bertiniani, Fuldenses); after 850 perhaps a Scandinavian smith here (H9.html). That they sold ships is ours (?)

sayings.text: A tenth to the king. The rest is yours, if the river lets you keep it.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the spine's tone line for a Frisian toll man); the tenth: the precept of 828

sayings.text: What is the good of those little napkins? I cannot cover myself with them in bed.
sayings.source: The emperor Charles, on Frisians selling short cloaks at the long price: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34, tr. A. J. Grant 1905, shortened

sayings.text: Hoist sail and flee Dorestad: the black merchant will give you no roof.
sayings.source: Alcuin, carmen 4, on Hrotberct, c. 780 (MGH Poetae I 220-223), our rendering

sayings.text: Frisia pours neither oil nor wine. That is why we carry them.
sayings.source: The first half is Alcuin's, carmen 4 (our rendering); the second is invented in the period's manner

sayings.text: A better burden may no man bear for wanderings wide than wisdom; worse food for the journey he brings not afield than an over-drinking of ale.
sayings.source: Hávamál 11, tr. H. A. Bellows 1923 (texts_793.json havamal_011): Ravn's, in Aldswith's house

sayings.text: The river gives a dam and takes a dam.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the dams were lengthened as the Rhine moved away (Van Es and Verwers)
invented: the toll man's, on tapping casks for blades (the ban on mail leaving the realm, Herstal 779)

sayings.text: Dorestad has fifty-five churches, said the monk. He had counted four, and a wet thumb did the rest.
sayings.source: A joke on Odbert's 55 churches (11th century), perhaps IV misread as LV: http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/H6.html. Invented in a scribe's manner

sayings.text: Three things come up this river unasked: the flood, the bishop's clerk and the Danes. The clerk at least goes home.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, a triad; for the years after 834
Alcuin's greeting to the bishop of Utrecht, 'vaccipotens', carmen 4 (our rendering): what Dorestad men call anyone from down the river

easter_eggs.text: In a cask-lined well at De Heul somebody has dropped, or hidden, a round gold brooch as broad as a hand, set with garnets, glass and pearls. It has nail holes in it: it was once nailed to something holy. Nobody comes back for it. It lies there until 1969.
easter_eggs.source: The Dorestad brooch, 8.4 cm, c. 775-800, found in 1969 in a well: https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula_van_Dorestad

easter_eggs.text: The priest at the upper church speaks of a bishop called Thuitbert who owned a very old book of the Roman Livy and wrote his name in it: 'of Thuitbert, bishop of Dorostat'. Nobody at Utrecht can say for certain who he was.
easter_eggs.source: The 8th-century owner's note in a 5th-century Livy, Vienna, Cod. Lat. 15: http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html

easter_eggs.text: A boy in Aldswith's house plays a flute made from the wing bone of a swan. The gaming pieces on her table are amber.
easter_eggs.source: A swan-bone flute, amber gaming pieces and lyre bridges from the excavations: http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/H9.html

easter_eggs.text: Three small white shells with a slit like a mouth hang on a string in a bead maker's door. He had them from a man who had them from a man. They come from a sea so far south that no one here has a name for it.
easter_eggs.source: Three cowries from the Red Sea or Indian Ocean found at Dorestad (Research/dorestad_c800_notes.md)

easter_eggs.text: From 812 the new penny shows a ship with the town's name round it. If you built a sea-going ship on the breaking beach, Gerbrand says the die cutter sat on a cask one whole day drawing her.
easter_eggs.source: The ship deniers of Dorestad, 812-818, DORESTADO or DORESTATVS (B5.html); the rest is the chain harbour.chain_house_new_ship's

easter_eggs.text: On an old mound by the graves at De Heul a man lies with a sword whose hilt is silver washed with gold. The old people say he was the last here to be buried with his sword, and that the priest did not like it.
easter_eggs.source: A grave with a silver-gilt-hilted sword, c. 750-800; almost no grave goods after c. 750 (H10.html)

easter_eggs.text: They tell at the church that Saint Boniface once struck a prison door at Dorestad with a king's staff and the chains fell off every man inside. Nobody can show you the prison.
easter_eggs.source: Vita Dagoberti (10th century, LATER): http://www.dorestadonthuld.nl/A2.html. Told before its time here (?)

easter_eggs.text: Four pennies buys wine enough for a party of tired women. Aldswith's granddaughter will tell you so in the 850s, and that she poured it.
easter_eggs.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 20 (Robinson 1921): Catla's four denarii

unlocks.what: Thiadburg stands surety for the house
unlocks.how: Leave goods in her storehouse over a season and pay what you owe her on the day; or take up Radger's blood-price.
unlocks.gives: flag db_surety: the count's steward gives a delay past Michaelmas on her word; she lends up to half the worth of the goods under her seal

unlocks.what: The moneyer takes your word on foreign silver
unlocks.how: Bring Sigimar your old and foreign silver and not a Dane's scales, and show him his first dirham.
unlocks.gives: flag sv_moneyer_trusts: the mint's cut on your silver is halved; he tells you a week early when the coin changes

unlocks.what: Two years without the king's tenth at Dorestad
unlocks.how: Buy the money riddle from the mint's clerk and answer it to him.
unlocks.gives: riddle reward rw_toll_dorestad (riddle_symphosius_91_pecunia): 'toll none' at Dorestad for two years

unlocks.what: The freshest word on Dorestad's prices
unlocks.how: Answer the anchor riddle set by the merchant's son in Aldswith's house.
unlocks.gives: riddle reward rw_tip_dorestad (riddle_symphosius_61_ancora): every price here is sure for the day

unlocks.how: Be known in the port and pay the steward 400 d (the work dorestad.work.plot).
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_plot_dorestad: a stock, a winter berth, and ground for a storehouse, a well, a shed and a dam

unlocks.what: A berth at your own dam head
unlocks.how: Hold a plot and pay for the dam (the work dorestad.work.dam); lengthen it every twelve years.
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_work_dorestad_jetty: no waiting, loading in half the time

unlocks.what: A sea-going ship built on the breaking beach
unlocks.how: Bring Gerbrand a quarter of the price and fetch the oak, the iron and the sailcloth (the chain harbour.chain_house_new_ship).
unlocks.gives: flag unlock_ship_north_sea_merchant_ship, and a slip on the beach (unlock_work_dorestad_slip)

unlocks.what: A berth on Saint Martin's bank, free of the king's dues
unlocks.how: Carry the bishop's letters and sell him wax fairly until he takes the house for one of the saint's men (the chain harbour.chain_house_debt, the Saint Martin road).
unlocks.gives: No bank due and no 'giscot' at Dorestad, and no one may seize your goods there at your death; you pay the saint instead, and the count dislikes it

unlocks.how: Pay Aldgrim the tenth without a speech on five visits and never be caught short.
unlocks.gives: npc tollman feeling up: he does the Frank in front first, searches you last and lightest, and tells you who came in today

unlocks.what: The bench by the fire in Aldswith's house
unlocks.how: Pay your crew before they drink and never bring a fight under her roof.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging for the skipper; the pick of the men who want a berth; last night's talk each morning without paying for it

unlocks.how: From 850, pay Eystein the tenth without complaint and swear to his lord.
unlocks.gives: flag df_rorik_man: the toll eased while Rorik holds the town, and a warning before the flood winter of 863

unlocks.what: Your name said at the upper church
unlocks.how: Feed the poor in a hungry year, or pay for the house by the church (the work dorestad.work.hospice).
unlocks.gives: flag hy_fed_poor or unlock_work_dorestad_hospice: porters and the poor bring you word a day early; a grave by the church for you and your heirs
